title: The bees and the honey — no juice says "I am from this tree" (6.9)
hook: bees gather nectar from a hundred different trees, and in the honey, no drop can say which tree it came from

segments.voice: Yesterday: sleep, the bird on a string that comes back to where it's tied. Your line was rest is return. Did your mind land on one breath last night? Day three hundred forty-five.

Pick up a jar of honey. Wildflower, the label says. That means bees went out and visited clover, and dandelion, and an apple tree, and a lime tree, and a hundred other flowers you'll never know. They brought it all home and worked it together, and now it's one golden thing in a jar. Try to find the apple-tree part. You can't. It's not that it's gone. It's in there. It just can't be picked out anymore. Uddalaka, teaching his son, picks up the same jar.
screen: `WILDFLOWER HONEY.` → `CLOVER, DANDELION, APPLE, LIME.` → `FIND THE APPLE-TREE PART.`

segments.voice: Uddalaka says: just as bees make honey, my dear, by gathering the juices of many different trees and bringing them to a single sweetness, and in the honey those juices can't tell one another, I am the juice of this tree, I am the juice of that tree, in the same way, all these creatures, when they merge into Being, in deep sleep and at death, don't know: we have merged into Being. They don't keep their labels. Then he adds a line that's easy to skip, and shouldn't be. Whatever they are in this world, a tiger, a lion, a wolf, a boar, a worm, a moth, a gnat, a mosquito, they become that again. So the honey isn't the end of the story. Each one comes back as itself. Hold both halves. In the depth of Being, in the honey, the separate names are gone. And here, in the world, the tiger wakes up a tiger and the mosquito a mosquito. Uddalaka isn't saying your life doesn't matter. He's saying that underneath your name, your family, your whole history, there's one sweetness you share with everything that lives. And the thing is, from the inside, you can't feel the merging. No juice says, I've merged. You just sleep, and wake up, and go back to being yourself. Then, once again, the refrain: that subtle essence is the self of all this; that is the truth; that is the self; you are that, Shvetaketu. Please, sir, says the son, tell me more.
screen: `MANY JUICES, ONE SWEETNESS.` · `NO JUICE SAYS: I'M FROM THIS TREE.` · `THE TIGER WAKES UP A TIGER.` · `TELL ME MORE, SIR.` · then, large: `THE NAMES ARE GONE IN THE HONEY.`

segments.voice: Today's practice tastes the honey. Sit and settle. Think of a few very different people in your life: someone you love, someone who annoys you, someone you passed on the street today. See each one clearly, labels and all. Then, breath by breath, let the labels soften, the way juices soften into honey. Just people, breathing, as you are. Rest in that for a while. The bell holds the time.
The bees and the honey. Many juices, one sweetness: in Being, no creature says I came from this tree, and in the world, each comes back as itself.
screen: `THE BEES AND THE HONEY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the rivers lose their names, just as the juices lose their trees. Today, notice one place where many separate things become one: a crowd, a choir, a shared meal. Day three hundred forty-five.

screen: `DAY 345 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE RIVERS AND THE SEA.`

howItsDone: Vedanta teachers often take Uddalaka's lessons one at a time, as here, and the honey image is one of several the Chandogya uses for creatures merging into Being in sleep and death.

match.prompt: what's inside the lesson — tap the pairs.
pairs: can't say which tree they're from

myth: in Uddalaka's lesson, merged creatures know they've merged into Being
no juice says it; no creature knows we have merged.
Uddalaka says creatures come back as what they were
a tiger, a lion, a wolf, a gnat: they become that again.
the lesson ends with the refrain you are that
tat tvam asi, again, and Shvetaketu asks for more.

fork.setup: you're a drop of nectar from an apple tree, now part of a jar of honey. someone asks where you came from. what can you say?
options: I'm from the apple tree, clearly.
nothing: in the honey, no juice can say which tree it came from.
fork.reveal: in the honey, the juices can't tell one another apart. so creatures, merged in Being, don't know they've merged.

original.note: Sanskrit madhu: honey, sweetness. the bees make madhu from many trees.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty image about honey.
what it means: in Being, the separate names dissolve; in the world, each one returns as itself.
what a scholar hears: Chandogya 6.9.1–4. the list of returning creatures (tiger, lion, wolf, boar, worm, moth, gnat, mosquito) keeps individuality in the world even as names merge in Being.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.9.1–4 (the bees and the honey; the returning creatures; the refrain)

notes: 'In deep sleep and at death' is a common reading of 'when they merge into Being' here (cf. 6.8 and 6.10); the text itself says 'merge into Being'. Confirm.
Creature list (tiger, lion, wolf, boar, worm, moth/fly, gnat, mosquito) per 6.9.3; translators vary on the insect names.

Carry 'the rivers lose their names' kept exactly as the index; it anticipates tomorrow's rivers (6.10). The voice ties it to today's image without teaching 6.10. Suggest the outline use 'the juices lose their trees' for this day.
